questions.text: When a Year 10 student sprints up a hill, the body reacts in several ways. Which of the following BEST describes how the circulatory and respiratory systems work together during the sprint?
options: Breathing rate increases to take in more oxygen, and the heart pumps faster to deliver that oxygen to working muscles and remove carbon dioxide
Breathing slows down so oxygen is used more efficiently, and the heart slows to save energy
Only the respiratory system is needed; the circulatory system stops during exercise
The digestive system supplies oxygen directly to the muscles
questions.expectedAnswer: Breathing rate increases to take in more oxygen, and the heart pumps faster to deliver that oxygen to working muscles and remove carbon dioxide
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer describes both systems working together.

Here's why:
During exercise, the muscles need more oxygen to release energy from glucose (aerobic respiration) and produce more carbon dioxide as a waste product.
The respiratory system increases breathing rate and depth to take in more oxygen and remove more CO2.
The circulatory system increases heart rate so oxygenated blood is pumped to the working muscles faster.
This is a common Year 10 application question — knowing the two systems are connected is key.

questions.text:
Read these four statements about a Year 10 student:

(i) Hīria visits her marae most weekends and feels strongly connected to her tūpuna.
(ii) Hīria walks to school every day and plays for the school netball team.
(iii) Hīria has a close group of friends and lives with her grandparents.
(iv) Hīria uses journaling to manage anxiety before exams.

Which dimension of Te Whare Tapa Whā does statement (i) MOST clearly describe?
options: Taha tinana
Taha hinengaro
Taha whānau
Taha wairua
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is Taha wairua.

Here's why:
Taha wairua (spiritual well-being) is about identity, meaning, purpose and connection — including connection to whenua (land), tūpuna (ancestors) and beliefs.
A marae visit and feeling connected to tūpuna fits taha wairua most closely.
Watch out: statement (iii) is taha whānau, (ii) is taha tinana, (iv) is taha hinengaro — students must distinguish carefully between the dimensions.

questions.text:
A Year 10 student is starting to date someone from another school. They notice their partner constantly texts to check up on them, gets angry if they don't reply within a few minutes, and tells them not to spend time with certain friends.

Identify TWO warning signs in this scenario, explain what makes each one unhealthy, and describe how it could affect the student's hauora.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark for each warning sign that includes both an explanation of WHY it is unhealthy AND a link to a hauora dimension. 2 required.

Examples of strong answers:

Controlling behaviour (telling them not to see friends) — this is a form of social isolation and removes the student's right to choose their own relationships. It damages taha whānau by cutting them off from friends and family support.

Constant monitoring (excessive texting and demanding instant replies) — this shows a lack of trust and pressures the student to always be available. It damages taha hinengaro because they feel anxious every time their phone is silent, and creates ongoing stress.

Anger when they don't reply — using anger to control behaviour is emotional manipulation. This damages taha hinengaro (anxiety, fear) and over time can damage taha wairua (loss of self-worth and identity).

Do NOT award the second mark if the student only describes one warning sign or fails to link it to hauora.

questions.text: Which statement BEST explains why nicotine vaping is particularly harmful for young people compared to adults?
options: Because young people's brains are still developing (until around age 25), and nicotine can affect brain development, memory, attention, and increase the risk of long-term addiction
Because vaping causes immediate heart attacks in anyone under 18
Because vaping is much more dangerous than smoking traditional cigarettes
Because vape devices are heavier than cigarettes and damage the lungs more
questions.expectedAnswer: Because young people's brains are still developing (until around age 25), and nicotine can affect brain development, memory, attention, and increase the risk of long-term addiction
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the first option.

Here's why:
The key reason vaping is particularly harmful for young people is that the adolescent brain is still developing.
Nicotine acts on developing brain pathways, can permanently affect attention, memory and impulse control, and rewires the reward system, leading to faster and stronger addiction in young people than in adults.
The other options are misconceptions — vaping does not cause immediate heart attacks, is generally less harmful than smoking but NOT harmless, and the device weight is not the issue.

questions.text:
A Year 10 student wants to improve their fitness for the school cross-country. They currently do no regular exercise. Describe TWO different components of fitness they should target, and for EACH component:
• describe a specific activity they could do
• explain how that activity improves that component
• link it to a dimension of hauora.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark per fitness component IF the answer includes all three parts (activity + how it improves the component + hauora link). 2 components required.

Examples of strong answers:

Cardiovascular endurance — Activity: jogging 3 km, three times a week, gradually building distance. How: the heart and lungs adapt to deliver oxygen more efficiently, so the student can sustain effort for longer in the cross-country. Hauora: supports taha tinana (fitter body) and taha hinengaro (stress relief from running).

Muscular endurance — Activity: bodyweight exercises like lunges and squats. How: leg muscles become better able to keep contracting without fatigue, so the student can climb hills in the cross-country without slowing. Hauora: supports taha tinana, and achieving small goals supports taha wairua (sense of progress and identity as 'an athlete').

Flexibility — Activity: 10 minutes of stretching after each run. How: increases joint range of motion, reducing injury risk. Hauora: supports taha tinana and taha hinengaro (mindfulness during stretching).

Do not award the mark for only naming the component.

questions.text: Which of the following is BEST described as a PROTECTIVE factor for mental health, rather than a risk factor?
options: Spending more than 5 hours a day comparing yourself to others on social media
Having at least one trusted adult and one close friend you can talk to honestly
Bottling up worries because 'other people have it worse'
Avoiding sleep so you have more time to study for exams
questions.expectedAnswer: Having at least one trusted adult and one close friend you can talk to honestly
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the second option.

Here's why:
Protective factors are things that REDUCE the chance of developing mental health problems and help people recover faster.
Having even one trusted person to talk to is one of the strongest protective factors for adolescent mental health.
The other options are all risk factors — social comparison, bottling up emotions, and sleep deprivation all increase the risk of poor mental health.

questions.text:
The chart above shows adult obesity rates by ethnicity in New Zealand.

(a) Calculate the percentage point difference between the HIGHEST group and the NZ Total. Then calculate how many times higher (as a ratio) the HIGHEST group's rate is compared to the LOWEST group's rate. Show your working.

(b) Explain TWO reasons why obesity is a significant health issue in New Zealand. At least ONE of your reasons must reference TWO different dimensions of hauora and show how they are linked.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark for part (a) — must include BOTH calculations correctly:

Difference: Pacific Peoples (highest) = 64%, NZ Total = 34%. Difference = 64 - 34 = 30 percentage points.

Ratio: Pacific Peoples 64% vs Asian (lowest) 16%. 64 ÷ 16 = 4. The highest group's rate is 4 times the lowest.

1 mark for part (b): TWO clear reasons, with at least ONE linking two hauora dimensions.

Example of a strong answer:

Reason 1: Obesity raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease and some cancers, putting strain on the public health system. This affects taha tinana (physical illness) AND taha hinengaro (anxiety and depression linked to chronic disease and bullying), showing how poor physical health drags down mental well-being.

Reason 2: Obesity in NZ is strongly linked to socioeconomic factors — families on lower incomes have less access to fresh food and safe spaces to exercise, so this is a community/equity issue, not just an individual one.

Do not award the second mark if no two-dimension hauora link is shown.

questions.text: Risk-taking behaviour is sometimes positive (e.g. trying out for a sports team) and sometimes harmful. Which of the following scenarios describes a HARMFUL risk-taking behaviour where a teenager is exposing OTHERS to harm, not just themselves?
options: Eating a new food at a friend's house for the first time
Speaking in front of the whole school assembly
Driving while distracted by a phone with friends in the car
Trying out for the school debating team
questions.expectedAnswer: Driving while distracted by a phone with friends in the car
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is driving while distracted with friends in the car.

Here's why:
This behaviour creates serious risk for OTHER people (passengers, other drivers, pedestrians) as well as the driver — that's the key part of the question.
Trying new food, public speaking, and trying out for a team are positive risks that build confidence and skills.
Distracted driving is the leading cause of crashes in teen drivers in NZ — a real-world Year 10 health topic.

questions.text: Choose ONE community-based health initiative in New Zealand (e.g. KickStart Breakfast, Water Safety NZ, the 1737 helpline, school counsellors, Pink Shirt Day, Movember). Describe how it works AND explain how it supports at least TWO dimensions of hauora for young people.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark for clearly naming and describing a real NZ initiative (what it does, who it serves).

1 mark for explaining how it supports AT LEAST TWO dimensions of hauora.

Example of a strong answer:

'KickStart Breakfast is a Sanitarium and Fonterra programme that provides free breakfast (Weet-Bix and milk) at primary and intermediate schools across NZ. It supports taha tinana because students start the day with fuel for learning and growing — without breakfast they can be tired and unwell. It also supports taha whānau because students eat together at school in a shared space, building a sense of community and reducing the stigma for kids whose families can't afford breakfast.'

Other valid examples:

1737 helpline (free text/call mental health support) — supports taha hinengaro and taha whānau.

Water Safety NZ school programmes — supports taha tinana (drowning prevention) and taha wairua (confidence in the water as part of NZ identity).

Do not award full marks if only one hauora dimension is mentioned, or if the initiative is not named/explained.

questions.text:
A new Year 10 student has moved to your school from another country. They speak some English but find it hard, are eating lunch alone, and have started missing school days.

(a) Use Te Whare Tapa Whā to explain how this situation could affect their well-being across ALL FOUR dimensions of hauora. Give a specific consequence for each dimension.
(b) Suggest TWO specific actions the school community could take to support them, and for each action explain which TWO dimensions of hauora it would most help and WHY.
questions.markingGuide:
Up to 2 marks for part (a) — must address all four dimensions with a specific, plausible consequence:

Taha whānau — separated from old friends/extended family, eating lunch alone, no sense of belonging at the new school.

Taha hinengaro — anxiety about being misunderstood, embarrassment about their English, sadness, possible signs of depression, school refusal.

Taha wairua — disconnected from culture, language and identity that gave their old life meaning; may feel they have lost their place in the world.

Taha tinana — stress can cause poor sleep and appetite, leading to fatigue, and missing school means less physical activity.

Award 1 mark for 3 dimensions explained well, 2 marks for all 4 dimensions explained well with specific consequences.

1 mark for part (b) — TWO specific actions, each with the TWO dimensions it most supports AND a justification.

Examples of strong actions:

Buddy system — pair the new student with a kind, bilingual or culturally aware student who eats lunch with them and walks them to class. Most supports taha whānau (rebuilds belonging) and taha hinengaro (less anxiety knowing they have someone).

Cultural sharing day or international club — invites the student to share food, music or photos from their home culture. Most supports taha wairua (reconnects them with identity and meaning) and taha whānau (helps the school community get to know them).

ESOL support classes / teacher check-ins — supports taha hinengaro (less stress about language) and taha tinana (improved attendance, regular routines).

Do NOT award the action mark unless BOTH actions identify TWO dimensions and explain why.
